paras: The Breaux Bridge night raid was an attack on the night of September 14, 1888, in which four or five armed men went to Black cabins near Breaux Bridge, Louisiana, killed a Black woman, whipped a Black man, and sexually assaulted a Black woman. Five men were arrested; one, Sam Polk, turned state's witness and named Vilmont Hollier as the man who fired, and two were held without bail. The killing was carried by wire across the country and was cited in the United States Senate as political violence.

According to the New Iberia Enterprise, the attackers had stolen cotton, and the dead woman's husband was the only witness against them. The Weekly Messenger of St. Martinville said the husband was the only witness in a pending case against Vilmont Hollier, a man pardoned by Governor McEnery months into a manslaughter sentence.

At about 11 o'clock that Friday night the band came to the couple's cabin and called for the husband, saying they were the sheriff. The woman opened the door, recognized one of the men, slammed it, and was shot through the abdomen. Her mother told a Times-Democrat correspondent that the man was Sam Polk. Before she died the woman made a deposition to Coroner Guilbeau, and the inquest found she was carrying twins of seven months, one struck in the head by the ball.

The same night a Black man was badly whipped and a Black woman "outraged," apparently by the same gang. A hat belonging to one of the attackers was found at the cabin and given to the district attorney.

The next night about 300 white men met and adopted resolutions pledging protection to the colored people and punishment of the perpetrators. On September 17 the husband and mother made affidavits against Polk, whom the Messenger called "a young white man of Breaux Bridge". Sheriff Gardemal and a posse then arrested Vilmont, Detour and Didier Hollier and Numa Boudreau.

The Messenger said the evidence would show that Vilmont Hollier had posed as "chief of patrol" and got the young men drunk in order to kill the husband. Polk, arrested on September 22, confessed and testified that Vilmont Hollier fired the fatal shots while he and Boudreau stood 30 or 40 paces away. Vilmont and Didier Hollier were remanded without bail, and the other three were released.
On September 25 Polk was arrested again on a charge of rape and released on a $1,000 bond. No report of an indictment or trial appears in the later coverage.

The first reports came from a Picayune special sent out on September 16 and 17, which described five "unknown" men. On September 17 it ran in the Savannah Morning News, the Washington Evening Star and the Camden Evening Telegram. Headlines ranged from "OUTRAGES AGAINST NEGROES" in Savannah and "Villainous Outrage in Louisiana" in Rock Island to "The Word of White Brutes" in Wilmington. The Yankton Press and Daily Dakotaian headed it "Southern Outrages and Negro Sufferers," and the Atlanta Constitution and the Richland Beacon ran the wire through September 25.

In Louisiana, the Times-Democrat's correspondent, reprinted in the Lake Charles Commercial, called it "one of the most cowardly crimes that ever was committed in this parish." The Messenger headed its report "Horrible Murder," followed the hearings weekly, and praised the sheriff's "great detective skill". The Opelousas Courier reprinted the Enterprise's cotton-theft explanation, with a French-language item to the same effect.

In the Senate, as the Concord Independent Statesman reported, Senator Chandler quoted the Picayune dispatches and predicted that "the indignation will end in resolutions," with no indictment. He argued that such outrages aimed to carry St. Martin Parish for the Democrats, and read the Louisiana Standard's account, headed "Democratic Murder—An Epidemic of Assassination".
The wire said the woman died a few hours after she was shot; her mother said the next morning. The wire counted five attackers, the Courier four or five, and the Messenger four.

Polk, himself accused, named Vilmont Hollier alone as the shooter, while the Enterprise said Vilmont and his son Detour fired. The Messenger and the Courier's French item named Didier rather than Detour as the son held without bail.

accounts.gist: Five unknown men shot through the walls of a Black cabin, killing a woman, then outraged a woman and whipped a man at another cabin; 300 whites met and pledged protection.

accounts.label: Dead woman's mother (Times-Democrat special)
accounts.gist: The gang said it was the sheriff; the woman opened the door, recognized Sam Polk, shut it, and was shot through the door; she died next morning.

accounts.label: Weekly Messenger
accounts.gist: The men called for the husband, apparently to whip him; the woman recognized one of four by moonlight and was shot with a rifle; Hollier posed as chief of patrol to kill the husband, a witness against him.

accounts.label: Sam Polk, state's witness
accounts.gist: Vilmont Hollier fired the fatal shots with Didier and Detour Hollier beside him while Polk and Boudreau stood 30 or 40 paces away; Detour took Polk's hat.

accounts.label: New Iberia Enterprise
accounts.gist: Cotton thieves raided to kill the husband, the only witness against them; Vilmont Hollier and his son Detour did the shooting.

accounts.label: Senator Chandler
accounts.gist: The outrages were part of a system of terror to carry St. Martin Parish for the Democrats, and the indignation would end in resolutions without punishment.

framing.detail: National papers ran the wire under headlines such as 'OUTRAGES AGAINST NEGROES', 'Villainous Outrage in Louisiana' and 'An Awful Crime', stressing the white indignation meeting.
The Wilmington Daily Republican headed the wire 'The Word of White Brutes' and the Yankton paper 'Southern Outrages and Negro Sufferers'.
The Times-Democrat special called it 'one of the most cowardly crimes' in the parish; the Lake Charles Commercial headed it 'A Brutal Crime.'
The Weekly Messenger headed it 'Horrible Murder', followed the hearings, and praised the sheriff's 'detective skill'.
The Opelousas Courier summarized the crimes, arrests and the Enterprise's cotton-theft explanation without comment.
The Independent Statesman, under 'SOUTHERN OUTRAGES', reported Chandler's charge that the killing was political terror by Democrats.
